newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania president to call election in new crisis.
newsitem.headline: Albania president to call election in new crisis.

text.p: Albania seemed on the brink of fresh turmoil on Wednesday as the president said he would call new elections and most political parties threatened to boycott the vote.
European envoy Franz Vranitzky prepared to race back to the Balkan state for his second visit in a week to try to defuse the new crisis.
Early elections have been planned since March, when a government of national unity was formed to stem the riots and violence which erupted in Albania after the collapse of pyramid investment schemes.
The threatened boycott would turn the election into a mockery.
President Sali Berisha said he would dissolve parliament and set June 29 as the election day.
"The day of June 29 will be one of the deepest victories of Albanian democracy," he told a crowd in the town of Kavaja, 50 km (30 miles) from Tirana and a stronghold of his support.

The fresh crisis blew up after Berisha's Democratic Party, which has an overwhelming parlaiemtnary majority, pushed through an election law which the other eight parties in the Government of National Reconciliation said favoured the former ruling party.
A dispute between the Democrats and the rest of the government over how many seats would be chosen by proportional representation and how many by majority had been bubbling on for weeks.
"We go to the elections sure that we will win and have one of the biggest victories for Albanian democracy," Berisha said.
The other parties in the government were meeting, trying to decide whether to carry out their threat to boycott the poll and hoping for the intervention of the West.
Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, a Socialist, has been in Washington since the latest crisis exploded but was expected back in Albania in the early afternoon.
The election law was a key element of a six-point political contract brokered by Vranitzky last week and signed by the Democrats and the eight other government parties.

The passing of the Democrats' own draft was seen as a snub to the Organisation for Security and Cooperation and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which Vranitzky represents. Vranitzky was due to return to Tirana on Thursday for a one-day visit.
The Democratic Party insisted its law was in line with the Vranitzky deal and agreements with the other parties.
It said it had to pass a law on Tuesday so Berisha had time to call the elections. Under Albanian law, the president has to call the vote at least 45 days before the elections.
"In amendments presented yesterday, all recommendations of the Council of Europe and the OSCE on improving many aspects of the elections...were included," the party said in a statement.
The Socialists pulled out of the last elections in May 1996. International observers said the vote was flawed.

Another key point of the Vranitzky contract was the disbanding of so-called salvation committees, formed mostly in the south of the country at the time of the rioting to bring back order as the state administration collapsed.
The contract stipulated they should disband 46 days before the electiion, but they have said they will break up only if the elections are guaranteed to be free and fair.
A meeting of the committees is due on May 16, where they will discuss whether to disband or not.
